verdict.rationale: The stem bundles two claims the vocabulary does not bundle. The equal worth half rests on stable lexical ground: Genesis 1:27 places both male and female under one image (tselem) of God without grading, 1 Peter 3:7 calls the wife a joint heir (syngkleronomos), and Galatians 3:28 denies a male and female divide in Christ using the paired Greek words for male (arsen) and female (thelys). The role distinction half turns on lexically open terms: head (kephale) carries two attested senses (authority over and source) that context does not disambiguate, and the verb at 1 Timothy 2:12 (authentein) is a hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament) whose sense cannot be triangulated from one occurrence. Two coherent readings arise from the identical word stock, so the conjunction is materially contested at the text level.

scripture.force: Both male (zakar) and female (neqebah) are placed under one and the same image (tselem) of God in a single clause, with no modifier grading the image by sex. The Hebrew supplies no lexeme (word) that ranks the dignity of the sexes at the creation root, which fixes equal worth at the canon's opening.

The woman is called a helper corresponding to him (ezer kenegdo). The noun helper (ezer) is used elsewhere of God himself as Israel's helper (Exodus 18:4, Deuteronomy 33:7, 33:26, 33:29, Psalm 33:20, Psalm 121:1-2, Psalm 124:8, Psalm 146:5), so the term lexically cannot encode inferiority. The phrase asserts complementary fit without ranking, and the word does not by itself fix the question of role.

The clause "there is no male and female in Christ Jesus" (ouk eni arsen kai thely en Christo Iesou) negates the male and female divide in Christ Jesus. The same paired sequence (no Jew nor Greek, no slave nor free, no male and female) groups three distinctions whose practical scope the words do not separately rank, so whether the abolition reaches household and assembly role as well as standing in salvation (soteriological standing) is exactly what the lexeme (word) leaves open.

A three link chain places the head (kephale) of every man as Christ, the head (kephale) of woman as the man, and the head (kephale) of Christ as God. Because the same noun governs the Father and Christ relation (where essential subordination is excluded by the canon elsewhere), the term cannot by itself encode ranking of essence, and lexically it carries two attested senses, authority over and source or origin. The verse asserts an ordered relation but the precise force of head (kephale) is not settled by the word alone.

The participle "submitting to one another in the fear of Christ" (hypotassomenoi allelois en phobo Christou) governs the household section. Ephesians 5:22 carries no second verb in the best textual witnesses, and grammatically borrows the participle from verse 21. Whether the wife specific application in verse 22 narrows the participle or merely instances a general mutual posture is the syntactic crux (the central grammatical puzzle), and the construction permits both.

The husband is named head (kephale) of the wife as Christ is head (kephale) of the church, his body (soma), and is at once called savior (soter) of that body. The head and body imagery binds the two parties into one organism rather than ranking two separable agents, so the verse supports an ordered pairing yet resists a bare command and control reading.

Husbands are commanded to love (agapate) their wives just as (kathos) Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The imperative assigned to the husband is self giving sacrifice ("he gave himself up," paredoken heauton), not dominance, so whatever ordering the passage sets up is defined by costly love rather than by privilege.

Paul does not permit a woman to teach (didaskein) or to exercise authority (authentein) over a man. The verb "to exercise authority" (authentein) is a hapax legomenon (a word occurring only once in the entire New Testament), occurring only here in the entire canon, and its sense in attested koine (common Greek of the New Testament era) ranges from to hold authority to to domineer or usurp. A single occurrence cannot triangulate which sense Paul invokes, so the verse clearly restricts something but whether it bars a settled office or an abusive seizure of control is lexically underdetermined (not pinned down by the words alone).

The rationale "for Adam was formed first, then Eve" (Adam gar protos eplasthe, eita Heua) grounds the preceding restriction in creation order. The conjunction "for" (gar) marks a causal link, but the word "first" (protos) by itself encodes temporal sequence without necessarily encoding hierarchy, and whether priority of formation entails priority of role is what the proposition tests.

The overseer must be "a one woman man" (mias gynaikos andra) and manage his own (idiou) household. The qualifying phrase is grammatically male coded, which one role distinction reading takes as legislating a sex distinction in the office, though the phrase primarily targets marital fidelity and the male coding may reflect the predominant local pattern rather than a transcultural sex bar.

Husbands are to grant honor to wives as joint heirs (synkleronomoi) of the grace of life, while the wife is called the "weaker vessel" (asthenesteros skeuos). The same clause asserts shared inheritance status and a functional or physical distinction in one breath, anchoring the equal worth claim while leaving the relational ordering open to either a hierarchical or a mutualist reading.

The verb "to exercise authority over" (exousiazo) is applied reciprocally: the wife does not have authority ("does not exercise authority," ouk exousiazei) over her own body but the husband does, and likewise (homoios), the husband does not have authority over his own body but the wife does. Where Paul wants to assign mutual authority he uses the verb "to exercise authority" (exousiazo) with explicit symmetry, which lexically contrasts with the singular verb "to exercise authority" (authentein) in 1 Timothy 2:12 and is part of why the canon's authority vocabulary resists a single uniform pattern.

complicating_texts.resolution: Galatians 3:28 negates the male and female divide "in Christ Jesus" (en Christo Iesou). Set in the context of salvation (justification and inheritance), the clause does not by its own wording cancel role language elsewhere, but the same clause yokes male/female with Jew/Greek and slave/free, and the words do not separately rank how far the abolition reaches. It is the strongest lexical anchor for equal worth and is read by one defensible lens as also flattening role distinction.

Genesis 1:27 places both male and female in the image (tselem) of God, with no qualifier grading the image by sex. This fixes equal worth at the creation root and constrains any role reading to one that preserves equal dignity, but it does not itself address role ordering and does not by its own vocabulary foreclose role distinction either.

The phrase "helper corresponding to him" (ezer kenegdo) describes the woman as a corresponding helper, and the same noun "helper" (ezer) is used of God himself as Israel's helper across the Psalter and Deuteronomy. The lexeme (word) therefore cannot encode inferiority. The phrase asserts complementary fit, and the words do not rank whether the relation is ordered or symmetrical.

The hapax legomenon "to exercise authority" (authentein), a word occurring only once in the entire New Testament, cannot be resolved from a single canonical occurrence. The lexical store offers no second New Testament instance to triangulate the sense; the lexically symmetric mutual authority verb "to exercise authority" (exousiazo) at 1 Corinthians 7:4 sits in a different domain (the marriage bed) and cannot substitute. Whether 1 Timothy 2:12 reflects a permanent office distinction or a situational corrective against domineering teachers remains undetermined within the lexical evidence alone.

The verb "to exercise authority" (exousiazo) is applied reciprocally to husband and wife over each other's bodies. The reciprocity does not by itself overturn ordering language in Ephesians 5 or 1 Timothy 2 (the domain is the marital body, not teaching authority), but it shows the canon's authority vocabulary is not uniformly asymmetrical. The complication is acknowledged and the domain difference is the lexical bound.

variant_units_examined.note: The apparatus markers (textual variant notes) in the supplied text bracket a word order cluster around "to teach" (didaskein) and "to exercise authority" (authentein). The reordering does not change which acts are restricted, so the impact on the verdict is minor, but it confirms the clause sits in a textually noted zone.

Manuscript witnesses divide on whether Ephesians 5:22 carries an explicit imperative "submit" (hypotassesthe) or borrows the participle "submitting" (hypotassomenoi) from verse 21. The shorter reading is preferred by modern critical editions and sharpens the dependence on verse 21 mutual submission, but the verdict does not turn on this because the same dispute on scope persists either way.

variants.note: The bundle reports no ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) variant units within scope. The 1 Timothy word order and Ephesians 5:22 verb presence notes rest on standard apparatus signals in the supplied text, not on CBGM (Coherence Based Genealogical Method) data.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads head (kephale) as authority over (the canon repeatedly pairs it with body and ordering language), takes the 1 Timothy 2:13 creation order ("Adam was formed first," Adam protos eplasthe) as a transcultural rationale that grounds the 2:12 restriction beyond any local situation, treats the male coded overseer qualifications in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 as legislating a sex distinction in the office, and holds equal worth (Genesis 1:27, Galatians 3:28, 1 Peter 3:7 joint heirs, synkleronomoi) and distinct roles together as jointly affirmed.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: affirms equal worth, denies fixed role distinction
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads head (kephale) as source or origin (the same noun governs the Father and Christ relation, where ranking of essence is excluded), takes Ephesians 5:21 "submitting to one another" (hypotassomenoi allelois) as the controlling participle for the whole household section so verse 22 is one instance of mutual submission, reads the verb "to exercise authority" (authentein) as a corrective against domineering or usurping teachers in the Ephesian situation (not a bar on settled office), notes Galatians 3:28 yokes male and female with slave and free (the latter presumed now abolished), and points to women in New Testament ministry (Phoebe as servant or deacon (diakonos) in Romans 16:1, Junia among the apostles in Romans 16:7, Priscilla teaching Apollos in Acts 18:26, daughters prophesying in Acts 21:9, women praying and prophesying in 1 Corinthians 11:5) as canon data the role distinction reading must absorb. On this lens equal worth stands but a permanent role distinction is not lexically secured.

hermeneutics.notes: The two lenses draw opposite conclusions from the same lexical stock (the shared pool of original-language words) because the load bearing terms head (kephale) and "to exercise authority" (authentein) are semantically open and the canon supplies two patterns the words do not rank: ordering language (household codes, 1 Timothy 2:12, overseer qualifications) and equality and shared agency language (Genesis 1:27, Galatians 3:28, 1 Peter 3:7, women in ministry texts). The equal worth clause is not contested between the lenses; the role distinction clause is.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Men and women share equal worth and dignity before God. The biblical texts on household and gathered church order assign relational instructions whose force, whether a permanent role distinction or a context bound application, is contested at the level of the words themselves.
stem_audit.notes: The phrase "distinct, complementary roles" in the stem embeds the complementarian conclusion by naming the roles as fixed and complementary; the egalitarian reader denies that lexical fixity, not equal worth. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form separates the uncontested equal worth claim from the contested role ordering claim so neither lens is loaded by the question.

lay_summary: This proposition joins two claims that the words carry very differently, and that is the whole story. The first claim, that men and women are equal in worth and dignity before God, sits on firm lexical ground. Genesis 1:27 places both male and female under one and the same image (tselem) of God with no term grading that image by sex. 1 Peter 3:7 calls the wife a joint heir (synkleronomos) of the grace of life, a noun the canon uses elsewhere only for shared inheritance status (Romans 8:17, Ephesians 3:6, Hebrews 11:9). Galatians 3:28 denies a male and female divide in Christ using the paired Greek words for male (arsen) and female (thelys). No canonical word ranks the sexes in dignity. The second claim, that distinct and complementary roles are fixed for household and gathered church, depends on terms whose sense the words alone do not settle. The key noun head (kephale) in 1 Corinthians 11:3 and Ephesians 5:23 is read in attested usage either as authority over or as source and origin, and the same noun governs the relation of God to Christ, so it cannot by itself encode a ranking of essence. The crucial verb in 1 Timothy 2:12, "to exercise authority" (authentein), occurs only once in the whole canon, a hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament), and a single instance cannot fix whether Paul bars holding settled authority or bars domineering and usurping. Ephesians frames the household section with mutual submission in verse 21 before addressing wives, and commands husbands to love by self sacrifice rather than to rule. The overseer qualifications are phrased in male coded language, which one reading takes as legislating a sex distinction and another takes as targeting marital fidelity. Where Paul wants reciprocal authority, as in 1 Corinthians 7:4, he uses the verb "to exercise authority" (exousiazo) symmetrically, so the canon's authority vocabulary is not uniformly asymmetrical. Two coherent readings, one ordered and one mutualist, arise from the identical word stock. The role distinction half is therefore materially contested at the text level while the equal worth half is not, and the combined statement reads as disputed.
